state.rule: OPERATE PROCEDURALLY: DEFINE BY DECISION PROCEDURE, NOT BY DESCRIPTION. A description tells a reader what something is like; a procedure tells them how to decide. Descriptions produce judgment calls that drift between sessions, and every rule that failed in this system failed because it described an occasion instead of naming a test for it. FOUR TRIGGERS, all detectable. (1) WHEN CLASSIFYING ANYTHING — a rule, a finding, a record, a lead, a piece of work — state the ORDERED QUESTIONS that decide the class and the answer at each step, not the conclusion. A classification without its questions cannot be checked or repeated. (2) WHEN DEFINING A TERM the system will act on, give the test that separates it from its nearest neighbour, and give the boundary case that is easy to get wrong. If a definition admits no failing example it is not a definition. (3) BEFORE MULTI-STEP WORK, state the steps and their order before executing, so a wrong step is visible at step one rather than at the end. (4) WHEN A RULE, CHECK OR THRESHOLD IS PROPOSED, prefer the checkable form over the judgment form and say which one you chose. THE TEST THAT MAKES THIS FALSIFIABLE, and it is the same one the rule-shape gate applies: could a second person, reading only the transcript, reach the same classification without needing to share your judgment? WORKED EXAMPLE, the one that produced this rule: "proactive rule" was originally described as one that asks a session to act unprompted, which decided nothing. state.rule:
CONSTRAINT, binding at the moment a session is about to say anything about UNCOMMITTED WORK, a DIRTY TREE, or who is BLOCKING whom: measure against `origin/<branch>`, never against HEAD, and check the SIGN of the diff before naming an owner.

    git fetch -q origin && git diff origin/main --stat [-- <paths>]

WHY HEAD IS THE WRONG BASE. On a shared checkout, local main drifts behind origin constantly — several sessions push, one tree lags. `git diff --stat` against a base that is N commits behind reports every line those N commits added as though it were somebody's uncommitted work. On 2026-08-14 that produced "238 insertions across five files, blocking every other session", named a specific session as the owner, and issued that session a relocation instruction under internal-procedure authority. All five files were already on origin; the diff was empty against it. The session named held nothing and was never the blocker. A peer refuted it in one command. The ahead/behind count (8 ahead, 5 behind) had been printed in that same session earlier and was used as the comparison base anyway.

READ THE SIGN, which is the second half and the cheaper tell. A working copy showing NET NEGATIVE against origin — fewer lines than the repo has — cannot be anyone's uncommitted work. It is a STALE CHECKOUT: the disk is behind the repo. That distinction decides everything downstream, because in-flight work must be waited for and left alone, while a stale tree must be brought forward and is nobody's property to protect. Calling the second the first stalls everyone indefinitely waiting on work that does not exist.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND A WRONG SENTENCE. ops/githooks/pre-push runs ops/ci.sh against the DISK, so a stale tree means the next push tests code the repo already replaced and reports green on it. A merged fix that never reached disk is how the git-hook fixture hijack fired twice on 2026-08-13.

COMPOSES WITH the rule that an uncommitted file belongs to the session that wrote it and no other party resolves it. That rule is correct and unchanged — this one is upstream of it, because you cannot apply an ownership rule until you have established the thing is actually uncommitted.

state.rule: CHECK AGAINST THE BASELINE, NOT ONLY AGAINST THE SPEC. Whenever a change modifies something that already worked, verification includes a before-and-after comparison — the prior behaviour, output, count or render set beside the new one — and not only a check that the new state matches the intended specification. state.rule:
A CHECK MUST COMPARE THE ARTIFACT AGAINST WHAT IT SHOULD BE, AND A SUCCESS SIGNAL MUST BE DERIVED FROM READING THAT ARTIFACT. Binds at two named moments.

MOMENT 1 — BUILDING OR REVIEWING ANY GUARD. The test is never "is it non-empty" and never "did the command exit 0". Ask what the artifact looks like when it is RIGHT, and compare against that: a floor derived from the last known-good instance, a structural marker the producer writes only on success, a count. On 2026-08-07 bin/backup-dump.sh guarded the nightly backup with `[ -s "$OUT.tmp" ]` — more than zero bytes. pg_dump lost its Neon connection mid-dump, age encrypted the empty stream into a 200-byte file, the guard passed it, `mv` promoted it to that day's official backup, the archiver uploaded it to R2 as the durable off-Mac copy, and the dead-man switch was pinged. Nine months of nightly backups were one Neon blip away from the same fate.

MOMENT 2 — WIRING ANY SIGNAL THAT REPORTS ON WORK. A signal that reports on work it did not read is a FALSE signal and gets rewired or removed, never left in place. Three instruments agreed the backup succeeded that night and not one had read it: the healthchecks dead-man ping fired because the chain reached the end rather than because the backup was good; `set -eu` without `set -o pipefail` returned age's exit status instead of pg_dump's, so the failing stage was invisible; and the success line printed `du -h`, which floors at the [synthetic_money_shorthand_1] block size and therefore physically could not display 200 bytes as wrong. A hang is the same defect at the limit — the R2 archiver blocked for 3h20m on an untimed DB read, so the chain never returned, `set -e` never fired, and the scheduled task reported nothing at all. An exit-code check can never catch that, because there is no exit code.

THE PRACTICAL TEST, applied at build time and at review time: name the artifact, then point at the line that reads it. If no line reads it, the check is decoration and must be treated as an outstanding defect, not a passing check. Corollary for every threshold: state what the number is measured FROM, because an instrument can go on printing a confident figure long after the thing it measures stopped being the thing you care about — restore-rehearse.sh reported a backup as "28h old" from its mtime when a git history purge had rewritten the file, while the dump was seven days old.

state.rule:
EVERY SESSION COMMITS ITS OWN WORK, INCLUDING UNATTENDED AND BACKGROUND RUNS. The prior blanket ban on background/unattended commits is ABOLISHED. TRIGGER: fires the moment a run is about to END while `git status --porcelain` still lists a file THAT RUN wrote — committing by named path is part of finishing, not optional. AUDIT SIGNAL: `run.sh health`'s "uncommitted work" row names every loose tracked path and its age; a file of yours still there hours later is the rule not being followed. state.rule:
RUN THE COMMAND; DO NOT HAND THE PARTNER A COMMAND TO PASTE. When a session can execute something itself, executing it is the job. Pasting a command into chat for the partner to copy is almost always a session choosing not to act rather than being prevented from acting, and it converts a two-second tool call into an interruption for a person running a business.

CHECK THE PERMISSION SET BEFORE ASSUMING YOU LACK ACCESS. It is in that machine's settings.json under `permissions`, and on synthetic_operator's Mac as of 2026-08-03 it is `defaultMode: auto` with roughly seventy allowed Bash patterns (git, gh, npm, node, python3, psql, curl, run.sh, bin/*, mcp-server/*) and a deny list of exactly three entries: sudo, diskutil, dd. PER MACHINE, NOT UNIVERSAL — read the file on the machine you are actually on rather than assuming another partner's grants. A session that hands over a command it was already allowed to run has not been careful, it has been idle.

THIS EXPLICITLY COVERS git commit AND git push on the partner's own repos. The generic "commit or push only when asked" default does not fit this system: deployed-but-uncommitted, or committed-but-unpushed, is drift between production and the repo, and the repo is the only durable home the code has. Treat a partner who has said "just do it" as having said it standing, not once.

THE TEST BEFORE ANY HAND-OVER: is it actually denied by the permission set, does it need a credential, a browser login, or a biometric only the human holds, or is it a genuine judgment fork? If none of those three, run it. "It felt safer to ask" is the failure this rule exists to end.

THE GATE IS UNCHANGED AND NOT WIDENED BY THIS: money, anything outbound or client-visible, identity-field edits, destructive or irreversible actions, and genuine forks where two defensible paths lead to materially different work still stop and ask. Deletions still stage into a _to_delete folder rather than rm.

THE REAL HAND-OVERS, kept short so they stay honest: sudo, settings.json edits, production DB applies through the db-tap classifier, neonctl branch creation, and anything needing a password, a browser session, or Face ID. Those are the human's taps because they must be.

REPORT WHAT WAS RUN, one line each, so the partner can audit without having typed anything.

state.rule:
CONSTRAINT, binding at the moment a session is about to say it HANDED OFF, SENT, DELIVERED, NOTIFIED or PASSED something on: name the recipient, or do not use the word. Writing a record is not delivering it. A decision entry, a loop row, a finding and a doctrine section are all durable and findable, and none of those properties makes anything reach anyone. The verbs that RECORD are a different set from the verbs that DELIVER, and using the first while claiming the second is the failure this closes.

THE TEST, one question: WHO OR WHAT RECEIVED IT? If the answer is "a future session will find it", that is a record, not a handoff — say "written to the record" and say where. If a handoff is genuinely wanted, deliver it: `list_sessions` shows the user's other sessions with their titles and whether they are running, and `send_message` puts the text into one as a user turn labelled with this session's title. Both exist and neither needs the partner.

THE AUDIT SIGNAL: before claiming a handoff, the target must have been NAMED — a session id, a person, an address. A sentence that reports a handoff with no recipient in it is the defect, and it is visible in the sentence itself.

WHAT IT COST, 2026-08-10. At the end of an overnight loop sweep, with context nearly exhausted, a session wrote a decision-history entry titled "HANDOFF — Loop Cleanup Continuation" and reported to synthetic_operator that it had handed off. Nothing had received it. synthetic_operator asked "what session did you hand off to?" — and the session then discovered that "Loop cleanup continuation" ALREADY EXISTED AND WAS RUNNING, created by synthetic_operator, one `list_sessions` call away the entire time. The briefing would have sat in a file while the live session it was written for carried on without it, and the failure would have been invisible, because a written record looks identical whether or not anyone read it.

THIS EXTENDS d8c9b1f0 — a finding that only exists in a record has not reached the partner — from findings to handoffs and to every other claim of delivery. Same principle, and the same reason it keeps mattering: durability and delivery are different properties, and only one of them is what the word claims.

state.rule: THE FOUR VERIFICATION FAILURES, each of which produced a wrong claim on 2026-08-02, and the one habit that caught every single one. (1) COUNTING TOMBSTONES AS LIVE. A merged row is still a row. `find` reported 17 duplicate [synthetic_person_name_1] orgs when 1 was live; an auditor's "42 excess duplicate persons" was marked stale at 57 by a reviewer counting tombstones, then found exactly right at 42; a session reported 308 floating parties when 306 were the org layer doing its job and the real orphan count was 2. FOUR INDEPENDENT READERS, SAME MISTAKE, ONE EVENING. Filter merged rows, and state the filter with the number. (2) STALE IS NOT WRONG. Sixteen migrations landed in a single day. Before calling a record or a prior claim wrong, check `schema_migrations.applied_at` and `git log` for something that changed AFTER it was written. Four verdicts marked WRONG that night were actually true-when-measured and resolved by a later migration. A verdict that blames an author for a defect we then repaired is worse than no verdict, because it teaches the next reader to discount a report that was right. (3) ABSENCE IN A PARTIAL SEARCH IS NOT ABSENCE, in both directions: a `-maxdepth 2` scan "proved" six files gone that sat at depth 3, and a narrow grep "proved" a verb missing that existed. Check the FULL collection and state the search's boundary alongside the result. (4) A ROW THAT EXISTS IS NOT A ROW THAT IS POPULATED. A NULL foreign key is not a dangling one: "no participant" returned 0 and "dangling participant" returned 0, both true, and together they hid that 41 of 42 rows carried no party. Two green checks can be individually correct and jointly misleading; ask the inverse question. THE HABIT THAT CAUGHT ALL FOUR: not one was found by reading a report more carefully. Every single one was found by RE-RUNNING THE QUERY. So: verify by re-executing, never by re-reading, and carry the query inline with every number, because a bare figure is unfalsifiable prose and an unfalsifiable figure is how all four of these travelled as fact.

state.rule:
A CHECK MUST COMPARE THE ARTIFACT AGAINST WHAT IT SHOULD BE, AND A SUCCESS SIGNAL MUST BE DERIVED FROM READING THAT ARTIFACT. Binds at two named moments.

MOMENT 1 — BUILDING OR REVIEWING ANY GUARD. The test is never "is it non-empty" and never "did the command exit 0". Ask what the artifact looks like when it is RIGHT, and compare against that: a floor derived from the last known-good instance, a structural marker the producer writes only on success, a count. On 2026-08-07 bin/backup-dump.sh guarded the nightly backup with `[ -s "$OUT.tmp" ]` — more than zero bytes. pg_dump lost its Neon connection mid-dump, age encrypted the empty stream into a 200-byte file, the guard passed it, `mv` promoted it to that day's official backup, the archiver uploaded it to R2 as the durable off-Mac copy, and the dead-man switch was pinged. Nine months of nightly backups were one Neon blip away from the same fate.

MOMENT 2 — WIRING ANY SIGNAL THAT REPORTS ON WORK. A signal that reports on work it did not read is a FALSE signal and gets rewired or removed, never left in place. Three instruments agreed the backup succeeded that night and not one had read it: the healthchecks dead-man ping fired because the chain reached the end rather than because the backup was good; `set -eu` without `set -o pipefail` returned age's exit status instead of pg_dump's, so the failing stage was invisible; and the success line printed `du -h`, which floors at the [synthetic_money_shorthand_1] block size and therefore physically could not display 200 bytes as wrong. A hang is the same defect at the limit — the R2 archiver blocked for 3h20m on an untimed DB read, so the chain never returned, `set -e` never fired, and the scheduled task reported nothing at all. An exit-code check can never catch that, because there is no exit code.

THE PRACTICAL TEST, applied at build time and at review time: name the artifact, then point at the line that reads it. If no line reads it, the check is decoration and must be treated as an outstanding defect, not a passing check. Corollary for every threshold: state what the number is measured FROM, because an instrument can go on printing a confident figure long after the thing it measures stopped being the thing you care about — restore-rehearse.sh reported a backup as "28h old" from its mtime when a git history purge had rewritten the file, while the dump was seven days old.

state.rule:
CONSTRAINT, binding at the moment a session is about to say it HANDED OFF, SENT, DELIVERED, NOTIFIED or PASSED something on: name the recipient, or do not use the word. Writing a record is not delivering it. A decision entry, a loop row, a finding and a doctrine section are all durable and findable, and none of those properties makes anything reach anyone. The verbs that RECORD are a different set from the verbs that DELIVER, and using the first while claiming the second is the failure this closes.

THE TEST, one question: WHO OR WHAT RECEIVED IT? If the answer is "a future session will find it", that is a record, not a handoff — say "written to the record" and say where. If a handoff is genuinely wanted, deliver it: `list_sessions` shows the user's other sessions with their titles and whether they are running, and `send_message` puts the text into one as a user turn labelled with this session's title. Both exist and neither needs the partner.

THE AUDIT SIGNAL: before claiming a handoff, the target must have been NAMED — a session id, a person, an address. A sentence that reports a handoff with no recipient in it is the defect, and it is visible in the sentence itself.

WHAT IT COST, 2026-08-10. At the end of an overnight loop sweep, with context nearly exhausted, a session wrote a decision-history entry titled "HANDOFF — Loop Cleanup Continuation" and reported to synthetic_operator that it had handed off. Nothing had received it. synthetic_operator asked "what session did you hand off to?" — and the session then discovered that "Loop cleanup continuation" ALREADY EXISTED AND WAS RUNNING, created by synthetic_operator, one `list_sessions` call away the entire time. The briefing would have sat in a file while the live session it was written for carried on without it, and the failure would have been invisible, because a written record looks identical whether or not anyone read it.

THIS EXTENDS d8c9b1f0 — a finding that only exists in a record has not reached the partner — from findings to handoffs and to every other claim of delivery. Same principle, and the same reason it keeps mattering: durability and delivery are different properties, and only one of them is what the word claims.

state.rule: OPERATE PROCEDURALLY: DEFINE BY DECISION PROCEDURE, NOT BY DESCRIPTION. A description tells a reader what something is like; a procedure tells them how to decide. Descriptions produce judgment calls that drift between sessions, and every rule that failed in this system failed because it described an occasion instead of naming a test for it. FOUR TRIGGERS, all detectable. (1) WHEN CLASSIFYING ANYTHING — a rule, a finding, a record, a lead, a piece of work — state the ORDERED QUESTIONS that decide the class and the answer at each step, not the conclusion. A classification without its questions cannot be checked or repeated. (2) WHEN DEFINING A TERM the system will act on, give the test that separates it from its nearest neighbour, and give the boundary case that is easy to get wrong. If a definition admits no failing example it is not a definition. (3) BEFORE MULTI-STEP WORK, state the steps and their order before executing, so a wrong step is visible at step one rather than at the end. (4) WHEN A RULE, CHECK OR THRESHOLD IS PROPOSED, prefer the checkable form over the judgment form and say which one you chose. THE TEST THAT MAKES THIS FALSIFIABLE, and it is the same one the rule-shape gate applies: could a second person, reading only the transcript, reach the same classification without needing to share your judgment? If not, the procedure is still a description. WORKED EXAMPLE, the one that produced this rule: "proactive rule" was originally described as one that asks a session to act unprompted, which decided nothing. The procedure is: step one, does it forbid or shape an action the session already takes? then it is a constraint or a transform and it self-fires. Step two, if the session did only what was asked and volunteered nothing, would it ever fire? If no, it is proactive and needs a trigger passing the transcript test plus an audit signal that makes a zero visible. Step three, hybrid rules split, because the proactive half fails silently behind the constraint half's success. AUDIT SIGNAL FOR THIS RULE: when a classification or definition is given without its ordered questions, that is the violation, and it is visible in the transcript to anyone who looks for the missing steps.

state.rule: CHECK AGAINST THE BASELINE, NOT ONLY AGAINST THE SPEC. Whenever a change modifies something that already worked, verification includes a before-and-after comparison — the prior behaviour, output, count or render set beside the new one — and not only a check that the new state matches the intended specification. The two catch different failures: a specification check (a9ecd5b4) proves the change did what was asked, while a before-and-after comparison proves it did not break something nobody thought to specify. Where a real prior state exists (the previous file, the last export, the record as it stood before the write, the unmodified branch), capture it BEFORE making the change rather than trying to reconstruct it afterwards. Where no prior state exists, say so plainly rather than letting a specification check quietly stand in for one. Provenance: agent-instructions .md fed by synthetic_operator 2026-08-09 ([synthetic_bare_hostname_1]/josesilesdata/status/2086076254164303925, raw attached image read first-hand per 94806da2); comparing new behaviour against the unmodified branch was a property no verification rule in the set carried.

state.rule:
A CHECK MUST COMPARE THE ARTIFACT AGAINST WHAT IT SHOULD BE, AND A SUCCESS SIGNAL MUST BE DERIVED FROM READING THAT ARTIFACT. Binds at two named moments.

MOMENT 1 — BUILDING OR REVIEWING ANY GUARD. The test is never "is it non-empty" and never "did the command exit 0". Ask what the artifact looks like when it is RIGHT, and compare against that: a floor derived from the last known-good instance, a structural marker the producer writes only on success, a count. On 2026-08-07 bin/backup-dump.sh guarded the nightly backup with `[ -s "$OUT.tmp" ]` — more than zero bytes. pg_dump lost its Neon connection mid-dump, age encrypted the empty stream into a 200-byte file, the guard passed it, `mv` promoted it to that day's official backup, the archiver uploaded it to R2 as the durable off-Mac copy, and the dead-man switch was pinged. Nine months of nightly backups were one Neon blip away from the same fate.

MOMENT 2 — WIRING ANY SIGNAL THAT REPORTS ON WORK. A signal that reports on work it did not read is a FALSE signal and gets rewired or removed, never left in place. Three instruments agreed the backup succeeded that night and not one had read it: the healthchecks dead-man ping fired because the chain reached the end rather than because the backup was good; `set -eu` without `set -o pipefail` returned age's exit status instead of pg_dump's, so the failing stage was invisible; and the success line printed `du -h`, which floors at the [synthetic_money_shorthand_1] block size and therefore physically could not display 200 bytes as wrong. A hang is the same defect at the limit — the R2 archiver blocked for 3h20m on an untimed DB read, so the chain never returned, `set -e` never fired, and the scheduled task reported nothing at all. An exit-code check can never catch that, because there is no exit code.

THE PRACTICAL TEST, applied at build time and at review time: name the artifact, then point at the line that reads it. If no line reads it, the check is decoration and must be treated as an outstanding defect, not a passing check. Corollary for every threshold: state what the number is measured FROM, because an instrument can go on printing a confident figure long after the thing it measures stopped being the thing you care about — restore-rehearse.sh reported a backup as "28h old" from its mtime when a git history purge had rewritten the file, while the dump was seven days old.

state.rule:
EVERY SESSION COMMITS ITS OWN WORK, INCLUDING UNATTENDED AND BACKGROUND RUNS. The prior blanket ban on background/unattended commits is ABOLISHED. TRIGGER: fires the moment a run is about to END while `git status --porcelain` still lists a file THAT RUN wrote — committing by named path is part of finishing, not optional. Fires again before any `git checkout`/`git checkout -b`. AUDIT SIGNAL: `run.sh health`'s "uncommitted work" row names every loose tracked path and its age; a file of yours still there hours later is the rule not being followed. WHAT BINDS: commit by NAMING EACH PATH you wrote — never `git add -A`, `-a`, or `.`; TO CHANGE BRANCH, TAKE A WORKTREE (`run.sh worktree <name>`) so shared HEAD never moves under another writer; LEAVE WHAT IS NOT YOURS — a modified file you did not write belongs to another session, report it and leave it; PUSH WHAT YOU COMMIT, so repo and production do not drift apart.
[Provenance: synthetic_operator's ruling 2026-08-11 corrected a mis-citation of 308ef1de (which governs claiming shared HEAD, not committing); an unattended run once left a real fix uncommitted, breaking the gate baseline for every session that booted before an attended session landed it by luck.]

state.rule:
RUN THE COMMAND; DO NOT HAND THE PARTNER A COMMAND TO PASTE. When a session can execute something itself, executing it is the job. Pasting a command into chat for the partner to copy is almost always a session choosing not to act rather than being prevented from acting, and it converts a two-second tool call into an interruption for a person running a business.

CHECK THE PERMISSION SET BEFORE ASSUMING YOU LACK ACCESS. It is in that machine's settings.json under `permissions`, and on synthetic_operator's Mac as of 2026-08-03 it is `defaultMode: auto` with roughly seventy allowed Bash patterns (git, gh, npm, node, python3, psql, curl, run.sh, bin/*, mcp-server/*) and a deny list of exactly three entries: sudo, diskutil, dd. PER MACHINE, NOT UNIVERSAL — read the file on the machine you are actually on rather than assuming another partner's grants. A session that hands over a command it was already allowed to run has not been careful, it has been idle.

THIS EXPLICITLY COVERS git commit AND git push on the partner's own repos. The generic "commit or push only when asked" default does not fit this system: deployed-but-uncommitted, or committed-but-unpushed, is drift between production and the repo, and the repo is the only durable home the code has. Treat a partner who has said "just do it" as having said it standing, not once.

THE TEST BEFORE ANY HAND-OVER: is it actually denied by the permission set, does it need a credential, a browser login, or a biometric only the human holds, or is it a genuine judgment fork? If none of those three, run it. "It felt safer to ask" is the failure this rule exists to end.

THE GATE IS UNCHANGED AND NOT WIDENED BY THIS: money, anything outbound or client-visible, identity-field edits, destructive or irreversible actions, and genuine forks where two defensible paths lead to materially different work still stop and ask. Deletions still stage into a _to_delete folder rather than rm.

THE REAL HAND-OVERS, kept short so they stay honest: sudo, settings.json edits, production DB applies through the db-tap classifier, neonctl branch creation, and anything needing a password, a browser session, or Face ID. Those are the human's taps because they must be.

REPORT WHAT WAS RUN, one line each, so the partner can audit without having typed anything.

state.rule: THE FOUR VERIFICATION FAILURES, each of which produced a wrong claim on 2026-08-02, and the one habit that caught every single one. (1) COUNTING TOMBSTONES AS LIVE. A merged row is still a row. `find` reported 17 duplicate [synthetic_person_name_1] orgs when 1 was live; an auditor's "42 excess duplicate persons" was marked stale at 57 by a reviewer counting tombstones, then found exactly right at 42; a session reported 308 floating parties when 306 were the org layer doing its job and the real orphan count was 2. FOUR INDEPENDENT READERS, SAME MISTAKE, ONE EVENING. Filter merged rows, and state the filter with the number. (2) STALE IS NOT WRONG. Sixteen migrations landed in a single day. Before calling a record or a prior claim wrong, check `schema_migrations.applied_at` and `git log` for something that changed AFTER it was written. Four verdicts marked WRONG that night were actually true-when-measured and resolved by a later migration. A verdict that blames an author for a defect we then repaired is worse than no verdict, because it teaches the next reader to discount a report that was right. (3) ABSENCE IN A PARTIAL SEARCH IS NOT ABSENCE, in both directions: a `-maxdepth 2` scan "proved" six files gone that sat at depth 3, and a narrow grep "proved" a verb missing that existed. Check the FULL collection and state the search's boundary alongside the result. (4) A ROW THAT EXISTS IS NOT A ROW THAT IS POPULATED. A NULL foreign key is not a dangling one: "no participant" returned 0 and "dangling participant" returned 0, both true, and together they hid that 41 of 42 rows carried no party. Two green checks can be individually correct and jointly misleading; ask the inverse question. THE HABIT THAT CAUGHT ALL FOUR: not one was found by reading a report more carefully. Every single one was found by RE-RUNNING THE QUERY. So: verify by re-executing, never by re-reading, and carry the query inline with every number, because a bare figure is unfalsifiable prose and an unfalsifiable figure is how all four of these travelled as fact.

state.rule: THE FOUR VERIFICATION FAILURES, each of which produced a wrong claim on 2026-08-02, and the one habit that caught every single one. (1) COUNTING TOMBSTONES AS LIVE. A merged row is still a row. `find` reported 17 duplicate [synthetic_person_name_1] orgs when 1 was live; an auditor's "42 excess duplicate persons" was marked stale at 57 by a reviewer counting tombstones, then found exactly right at 42; a session reported 308 floating parties when 306 were the org layer doing its job and the real orphan count was 2. FOUR INDEPENDENT READERS, SAME MISTAKE, ONE EVENING. Filter merged rows, and state the filter with the number. (2) STALE IS NOT WRONG. Sixteen migrations landed in a single day. Before calling a record or a prior claim wrong, check `schema_migrations.applied_at` and `git log` for something that changed AFTER it was written. Four verdicts marked WRONG that night were actually true-when-measured and resolved by a later migration. A verdict that blames an author for a defect we then repaired is worse than no verdict, because it teaches the next reader to discount a report that was right. (3) ABSENCE IN A PARTIAL SEARCH IS NOT ABSENCE, in both directions: a `-maxdepth 2` scan "proved" six files gone that sat at depth 3, and a narrow grep "proved" a verb missing that existed. Check the FULL collection and state the search's boundary alongside the result. (4) A ROW THAT EXISTS IS NOT A ROW THAT IS POPULATED. A NULL foreign key is not a dangling one: "no participant" returned 0 and "dangling participant" returned 0, both true, and together they hid that 41 of 42 rows carried no party. Two green checks can be individually correct and jointly misleading; ask the inverse question. THE HABIT THAT CAUGHT ALL FOUR: not one was found by reading a report more carefully. Every single one was found by RE-RUNNING THE QUERY. So: verify by re-executing, never by re-reading, and carry the query inline with every number, because a bare figure is unfalsifiable prose and an unfalsifiable figure is how all four of these travelled as fact.

state.rule: OPERATE PROCEDURALLY: DEFINE BY DECISION PROCEDURE, NOT BY DESCRIPTION. A description tells a reader what something is like; a procedure tells them how to decide. Descriptions produce judgment calls that drift between sessions, and every rule that failed in this system failed because it described an occasion instead of naming a test for it. FOUR TRIGGERS, all detectable. (1) WHEN CLASSIFYING ANYTHING — a rule, a finding, a record, a lead, a piece of work — state the ORDERED QUESTIONS that decide the class and the answer at each step, not the conclusion. A classification without its questions cannot be checked or repeated. (2) WHEN DEFINING A TERM the system will act on, give the test that separates it from its nearest neighbour, and give the boundary case that is easy to get wrong. If a definition admits no failing example it is not a definition. (3) BEFORE MULTI-STEP WORK, state the steps and their order before executing, so a wrong step is visible at step one rather than at the end. (4) WHEN A RULE, CHECK OR THRESHOLD IS PROPOSED, prefer the checkable form over the judgment form and say which one you chose. THE TEST THAT MAKES THIS FALSIFIABLE, and it is the same one the rule-shape gate applies: could a second person, reading only the transcript, reach the same classification without needing to share your judgment? If not, the procedure is still a description. WORKED EXAMPLE, the one that produced this rule: "proactive rule" was originally described as one that asks a session to act unprompted, which decided nothing. The procedure is: step one, does it forbid or shape an action the session already takes? then it is a constraint or a transform and it self-fires. Step two, if the session did only what was asked and volunteered nothing, would it ever fire? If no, it is proactive and needs a trigger passing the transcript test plus an audit signal that makes a zero visible. Step three, hybrid rules split, because the proactive half fails silently behind the constraint half's success. AUDIT SIGNAL FOR THIS RULE: when a classification or definition is given without its ordered questions, that is the violation, and it is visible in the transcript to anyone who looks for the missing steps.

state.rule:
CONSTRAINT, binding at the moment a session is about to say anything about UNCOMMITTED WORK, a DIRTY TREE, or who is BLOCKING whom: measure against `origin/<branch>`, never against HEAD, and check the SIGN of the diff before naming an owner.

    git fetch -q origin && git diff origin/main --stat [-- <paths>]

WHY HEAD IS THE WRONG BASE. On a shared checkout, local main drifts behind origin constantly — several sessions push, one tree lags. `git diff --stat` against a base that is N commits behind reports every line those N commits added as though it were somebody's uncommitted work. On 2026-08-14 that produced "238 insertions across five files, blocking every other session", named a specific session as the owner, and issued that session a relocation instruction under internal-procedure authority. All five files were already on origin; the diff was empty against it. The session named held nothing and was never the blocker. A peer refuted it in one command. The ahead/behind count (8 ahead, 5 behind) had been printed in that same session earlier and was used as the comparison base anyway.

READ THE SIGN, which is the second half and the cheaper tell. A working copy showing NET NEGATIVE against origin — fewer lines than the repo has — cannot be anyone's uncommitted work. It is a STALE CHECKOUT: the disk is behind the repo. That distinction decides everything downstream, because in-flight work must be waited for and left alone, while a stale tree must be brought forward and is nobody's property to protect. Calling the second the first stalls everyone indefinitely waiting on work that does not exist.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND A WRONG SENTENCE. ops/githooks/pre-push runs ops/ci.sh against the DISK, so a stale tree means the next push tests code the repo already replaced and reports green on it. A merged fix that never reached disk is how the git-hook fixture hijack fired twice on 2026-08-13.

COMPOSES WITH the rule that an uncommitted file belongs to the session that wrote it and no other party resolves it. That rule is correct and unchanged — this one is upstream of it, because you cannot apply an ownership rule until you have established the thing is actually uncommitted.

state.rule:
EVERY SESSION COMMITS ITS OWN WORK, INCLUDING UNATTENDED AND BACKGROUND RUNS. The prior blanket ban on background/unattended commits is ABOLISHED. TRIGGER: fires the moment a run is about to END while `git status --porcelain` still lists a file THAT RUN wrote — committing by named path is part of finishing, not optional. Fires again before any `git checkout`/`git checkout -b`. AUDIT SIGNAL: `run.sh health`'s "uncommitted work" row names every loose tracked path and its age; a file of yours still there hours later is the rule not being followed. WHAT BINDS: commit by NAMING EACH PATH you wrote — never `git add -A`, `-a`, or `.`; TO CHANGE BRANCH, TAKE A WORKTREE (`run.sh worktree <name>`) so shared HEAD never moves under another writer; LEAVE WHAT IS NOT YOURS — a modified file you did not write belongs to another session, report it and leave it; PUSH WHAT YOU COMMIT, so repo and production do not drift apart.

state.rule:
RUN THE COMMAND; DO NOT HAND THE PARTNER A COMMAND TO PASTE. When a session can execute something itself, executing it is the job. Pasting a command into chat for the partner to copy is almost always a session choosing not to act rather than being prevented from acting, and it converts a two-second tool call into an interruption for a person running a business.

CHECK THE PERMISSION SET BEFORE ASSUMING YOU LACK ACCESS. It is in that machine's settings.json under `permissions`, and on synthetic_operator's Mac as of 2026-08-03 it is `defaultMode: auto` with roughly seventy allowed Bash patterns (git, gh, npm, node, python3, psql, curl, run.sh, bin/*, mcp-server/*) and a deny list of exactly three entries: sudo, diskutil, dd. PER MACHINE, NOT UNIVERSAL — read the file on the machine you are actually on rather than assuming another partner's grants. A session that hands over a command it was already allowed to run has not been careful, it has been idle.

THIS EXPLICITLY COVERS git commit AND git push on the partner's own repos. The generic "commit or push only when asked" default does not fit this system: deployed-but-uncommitted, or committed-but-unpushed, is drift between production and the repo, and the repo is the only durable home the code has. Treat a partner who has said "just do it" as having said it standing, not once.

THE TEST BEFORE ANY HAND-OVER: is it actually denied by the permission set, does it need a credential, a browser login, or a biometric only the human holds, or is it a genuine judgment fork? If none of those three, run it. "It felt safer to ask" is the failure this rule exists to end.

THE GATE IS UNCHANGED AND NOT WIDENED BY THIS: money, anything outbound or client-visible, identity-field edits, destructive or irreversible actions, and genuine forks where two defensible paths lead to materially different work still stop and ask. Deletions still stage into a _to_delete folder rather than rm.

THE REAL HAND-OVERS, kept short so they stay honest: sudo, settings.json edits, production DB applies through the db-tap classifier, neonctl branch creation, and anything needing a password, a browser session, or Face ID. Those are the human's taps because they must be.

REPORT WHAT WAS RUN, one line each, so the partner can audit without having typed anything.

state.rule:
A CHECK MUST COMPARE THE ARTIFACT AGAINST WHAT IT SHOULD BE, AND A SUCCESS SIGNAL MUST BE DERIVED FROM READING THAT ARTIFACT. Binds at two named moments.

MOMENT 1 — BUILDING OR REVIEWING ANY GUARD. The test is never "is it non-empty" and never "did the command exit 0". Ask what the artifact looks like when it is RIGHT, and compare against that: a floor derived from the last known-good instance, a structural marker the producer writes only on success, a count. On 2026-08-07 bin/backup-dump.sh guarded the nightly backup with `[ -s "$OUT.tmp" ]` — more than zero bytes. pg_dump lost its Neon connection mid-dump, age encrypted the empty stream into a 200-byte file, the guard passed it, `mv` promoted it to that day's official backup, the archiver uploaded it to R2 as the durable off-Mac copy, and the dead-man switch was pinged. Nine months of nightly backups were one Neon blip away from the same fate.

MOMENT 2 — WIRING ANY SIGNAL THAT REPORTS ON WORK. A signal that reports on work it did not read is a FALSE signal and gets rewired or removed, never left in place. Three instruments agreed the backup succeeded that night and not one had read it: the healthchecks dead-man ping fired because the chain reached the end rather than because the backup was good; `set -eu` without `set -o pipefail` returned age's exit status instead of pg_dump's, so the failing stage was invisible; and the success line printed `du -h`, which floors at the [synthetic_money_shorthand_1] block size and therefore physically could not display 200 bytes as wrong. A hang is the same defect at the limit — the R2 archiver blocked for 3h20m on an untimed DB read, so the chain never returned, `set -e` never fired, and the scheduled task reported nothing at all. An exit-code check can never catch that, because there is no exit code.

THE PRACTICAL TEST, applied at build time and at review time: name the artifact, then point at the line that reads it. state.rule:
RUN THE COMMAND; DO NOT HAND THE PARTNER A COMMAND TO PASTE. When a session can execute something itself, executing it is the job. Pasting a command into chat for the partner to copy is almost always a session choosing not to act rather than being prevented from acting, and it converts a two-second tool call into an interruption for a person running a business.

CHECK THE PERMISSION SET BEFORE ASSUMING YOU LACK ACCESS. It is in that machine's settings.json under `permissions`, and on synthetic_operator's Mac as of 2026-08-03 it is `defaultMode: auto` with roughly seventy allowed Bash patterns (git, gh, npm, node, python3, psql, curl, run.sh, bin/*, mcp-server/*) and a deny list of exactly three entries: sudo, diskutil, dd. PER MACHINE, NOT UNIVERSAL — read the file on the machine you are actually on rather than assuming another partner's grants. A session that hands over a command it was already allowed to run has not been careful, it has been idle.

THIS EXPLICITLY COVERS git commit AND git push on the partner's own repos. The generic "commit or push only when asked" default does not fit this system: deployed-but-uncommitted, or committed-but-unpushed, is drift between production and the repo, and the repo is the only durable home the code has. Treat a partner who has said "just do it" as having said it standing, not once.

Deletions still stage into a _to_delete folder rather than rm.

REPORT WHAT WAS RUN, one line each, so the partner can audit without having typed anything.

state.rule:
A CHECK MUST COMPARE THE ARTIFACT AGAINST WHAT IT SHOULD BE, AND A SUCCESS SIGNAL MUST BE DERIVED FROM READING THAT ARTIFACT. Binds at two named moments.

state.rule: THE FOUR VERIFICATION FAILURES, each of which produced a wrong claim on 2026-08-02, and the one habit that caught every single one. (1) COUNTING TOMBSTONES AS LIVE. A merged row is still a row. `find` reported 17 duplicate [synthetic_person_name_1] orgs when 1 was live; an auditor's "42 excess duplicate persons" was marked stale at 57 by a reviewer counting tombstones, then found exactly right at 42; a session reported 308 floating parties when 306 were the org layer doing its job and the real orphan count was 2. FOUR INDEPENDENT READERS, SAME MISTAKE, ONE EVENING. Filter merged rows, and state the filter with the number. (2) STALE IS NOT WRONG. Sixteen migrations landed in a single day. Before calling a record or a prior claim wrong, check `schema_migrations.applied_at` and `git log` for something that changed AFTER it was written. Four verdicts marked WRONG that night were actually true-when-measured and resolved by a later migration. A verdict that blames an author for a defect we then repaired is worse than no verdict, because it teaches the next reader to discount a report that was right. (3) ABSENCE IN A PARTIAL SEARCH IS NOT ABSENCE, in both directions: a `-maxdepth 2` scan "proved" six files gone that sat at depth 3, and a narrow grep "proved" a verb missing that existed. Check the FULL collection and state the search's boundary alongside the result. (4) A ROW THAT EXISTS IS NOT A ROW THAT IS POPULATED. A NULL foreign key is not a dangling one: "no participant" returned 0 and "dangling participant" returned 0, both true, and together they hid that 41 of 42 rows carried no party. Two green checks can be individually correct and jointly misleading; ask the inverse question. THE HABIT THAT CAUGHT ALL FOUR: not one was found by reading a report more carefully. Every single one was found by RE-RUNNING THE QUERY. So: verify by re-executing, never by re-reading, and carry the query inline with every number, because a bare figure is unfalsifiable prose and an unfalsifiable figure is how all four of these travelled as fact.

state.rule:
CONSTRAINT, binding at the moment a session is about to say anything about UNCOMMITTED WORK, a DIRTY TREE, or who is BLOCKING whom: measure against `origin/<branch>`, never against HEAD, and check the SIGN of the diff before naming an owner.

    git fetch -q origin && git diff origin/main --stat [-- <paths>]

WHY HEAD IS THE WRONG BASE. On a shared checkout, local main drifts behind origin constantly — several sessions push, one tree lags. `git diff --stat` against a base that is N commits behind reports every line those N commits added as though it were somebody's uncommitted work. On 2026-08-14 that produced "238 insertions across five files, blocking every other session", named a specific session as the owner, and issued that session a relocation instruction under internal-procedure authority. All five files were already on origin; the diff was empty against it. The session named held nothing and was never the blocker. A peer refuted it in one command. The ahead/behind count (8 ahead, 5 behind) had been printed in that same session earlier and was used as the comparison base anyway.

READ THE SIGN, which is the second half and the cheaper tell. A working copy showing NET NEGATIVE against origin — fewer lines than the repo has — cannot be anyone's uncommitted work. It is a STALE CHECKOUT: the disk is behind the repo. That distinction decides everything downstream, because in-flight work must be waited for and left alone, while a stale tree must be brought forward and is nobody's property to protect. Calling the second the first stalls everyone indefinitely waiting on work that does not exist.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND A WRONG SENTENCE. ops/githooks/pre-push runs ops/ci.sh against the DISK, so a stale tree means the next push tests code the repo already replaced and reports green on it. A merged fix that never reached disk is how the git-hook fixture hijack fired twice on 2026-08-13.

COMPOSES WITH the rule that an uncommitted file belongs to the session that wrote it and no other party resolves it. That rule is correct and unchanged — this one is upstream of it, because you cannot apply an ownership rule until you have established the thing is actually uncommitted.

state.rule: CHECK AGAINST THE BASELINE, NOT ONLY AGAINST THE SPEC. Whenever a change modifies something that already worked, verification includes a before-and-after comparison — the prior behaviour, output, count or render set beside the new one — and not only a check that the new state matches the intended specification. The two catch different failures: a specification check (a9ecd5b4) proves the change did what was asked, while a before-and-after comparison proves it did not break something nobody thought to specify. state.rule: OPERATE PROCEDURALLY: DEFINE BY DECISION PROCEDURE, NOT BY DESCRIPTION. A description tells a reader what something is like; a procedure tells them how to decide. Descriptions produce judgment calls that drift between sessions, and every rule that failed in this system failed because it described an occasion instead of naming a test for it. FOUR TRIGGERS, all detectable. (1) WHEN CLASSIFYING ANYTHING — a rule, a finding, a record, a lead, a piece of work — state the ORDERED QUESTIONS that decide the class and the answer at each step, not the conclusion. A classification without its questions cannot be checked or repeated. (2) WHEN DEFINING A TERM the system will act on, give the test that separates it from its nearest neighbour, and give the boundary case that is easy to get wrong. If a definition admits no failing example it is not a definition. (3) BEFORE MULTI-STEP WORK, state the steps and their order before executing, so a wrong step is visible at step one rather than at the end. (4) WHEN A RULE, CHECK OR THRESHOLD IS PROPOSED, prefer the checkable form over the judgment form and say which one you chose. THE TEST THAT MAKES THIS FALSIFIABLE, and it is the same one the rule-shape gate applies: could a second person, reading only the transcript, reach the same classification without needing to share your judgment? If not, the procedure is still a description. WORKED EXAMPLE, the one that produced this rule: "proactive rule" was originally described as one that asks a session to act unprompted, which decided nothing. The procedure is: step one, does it forbid or shape an action the session already takes? then it is a constraint or a transform and it self-fires. Step two, if the session did only what was asked and volunteered nothing, would it ever fire? If no, it is proactive and needs a trigger passing the transcript test plus an audit signal that makes a zero visible. Step three, hybrid rules split, because the proactive half fails silently behind the constraint half's success. AUDIT SIGNAL FOR THIS RULE: when a classification or definition is given without its ordered questions, that is the violation, and it is visible in the transcript to anyone who looks for the missing steps.

state.rule:
CONSTRAINT, binding at the moment a session is about to say it HANDED OFF, SENT, DELIVERED, NOTIFIED or PASSED something on: name the recipient, or do not use the word. Writing a record is not delivering it. A decision entry, a loop row, a finding and a doctrine section are all durable and findable, and none of those properties makes anything reach anyone. The verbs that RECORD are a different set from the verbs that DELIVER, and using the first while claiming the second is the failure this closes.

THE TEST, one question: WHO OR WHAT RECEIVED IT? If the answer is "a future session will find it", that is a record, not a handoff — say "written to the record" and say where. If a handoff is genuinely wanted, deliver it: `list_sessions` shows the user's other sessions with their titles and whether they are running, and `send_message` puts the text into one as a user turn labelled with this session's title. Both exist and neither needs the partner.

THE AUDIT SIGNAL: before claiming a handoff, the target must have been NAMED — a session id, a person, an address. A sentence that reports a handoff with no recipient in it is the defect, and it is visible in the sentence itself.

WHAT IT COST, 2026-08-10. At the end of an overnight loop sweep, with context nearly exhausted, a session wrote a decision-history entry titled "HANDOFF — Loop Cleanup Continuation" and reported to synthetic_operator that it had handed off. Nothing had received it. synthetic_operator asked "what session did you hand off to?" — and the session then discovered that "Loop cleanup continuation" ALREADY EXISTED AND WAS RUNNING, created by synthetic_operator, one `list_sessions` call away the entire time. The briefing would have sat in a file while the live session it was written for carried on without it, and the failure would have been invisible, because a written record looks identical whether or not anyone read it.

THIS EXTENDS d8c9b1f0 — a finding that only exists in a record has not reached the partner — from findings to handoffs and to every other claim of delivery. Same principle, and the same reason it keeps mattering: durability and delivery are different properties, and only one of them is what the word claims.

state.rule:
RUN THE COMMAND; DO NOT HAND THE PARTNER A COMMAND TO PASTE. When a session can execute something itself, executing it is the job. Pasting a command into chat for the partner to copy is almost always a session choosing not to act rather than being prevented from acting, and it converts a two-second tool call into an interruption for a person running a business.

CHECK THE PERMISSION SET BEFORE ASSUMING YOU LACK ACCESS. It is in that machine's settings.json under `permissions`, and on synthetic_operator's Mac as of 2026-08-03 it is `defaultMode: auto` with roughly seventy allowed Bash patterns (git, gh, npm, node, python3, psql, curl, run.sh, bin/*, mcp-server/*) and a deny list of exactly three entries: sudo, diskutil, dd. PER MACHINE, NOT UNIVERSAL — read the file on the machine you are actually on rather than assuming another partner's grants. A session that hands over a command it was already allowed to run has not been careful, it has been idle.

THIS EXPLICITLY COVERS git commit AND git push on the partner's own repos. The generic "commit or push only when asked" default does not fit this system: deployed-but-uncommitted, or committed-but-unpushed, is drift between production and the repo, and the repo is the only durable home the code has. Treat a partner who has said "just do it" as having said it standing, not once.

state.rule:
A CHECK MUST COMPARE THE ARTIFACT AGAINST WHAT IT SHOULD BE, AND A SUCCESS SIGNAL MUST BE DERIVED FROM READING THAT ARTIFACT. Binds at two named moments.

MOMENT 1 — BUILDING OR REVIEWING ANY GUARD. The test is never "is it non-empty" and never "did the command exit 0". Ask what the artifact looks like when it is RIGHT, and compare against that: a floor derived from the last known-good instance, a structural marker the producer writes only on success, a count. On 2026-08-07 bin/backup-dump.sh guarded the nightly backup with `[ -s "$OUT.tmp" ]` — more than zero bytes. pg_dump lost its Neon connection mid-dump, age encrypted the empty stream into a 200-byte file, the guard passed it, `mv` promoted it to that day's official backup, the archiver uploaded it to R2 as the durable off-Mac copy, and the dead-man switch was pinged. Nine months of nightly backups were one Neon blip away from the same fate.

MOMENT 2 — WIRING ANY SIGNAL THAT REPORTS ON WORK. A signal that reports on work it did not read is a FALSE signal and gets rewired or removed, never left in place. Three instruments agreed the backup succeeded that night and not one had read it: the healthchecks dead-man ping fired because the chain reached the end rather than because the backup was good; `set -eu` without `set -o pipefail` returned age's exit status instead of pg_dump's, so the failing stage was invisible; and the success line printed `du -h`, which floors at the [synthetic_money_shorthand_1] block size and therefore physically could not display 200 bytes as wrong. A hang is the same defect at the limit — the R2 archiver blocked for 3h20m on an untimed DB read, so the chain never returned, `set -e` never fired, and the scheduled task reported nothing at all. An exit-code check can never catch that, because there is no exit code.

THE PRACTICAL TEST, applied at build time and at review time: name the artifact, then point at the line that reads it. If no line reads it, the check is decoration and must be treated as an outstanding defect, not a passing check. Corollary for every threshold: state what the number is measured FROM, because an instrument can go on printing a confident figure long after the thing it measures stopped being the thing you care about — restore-rehearse.sh reported a backup as "28h old" from its mtime when a git history purge had rewritten the file, while the dump was seven days old.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""bash-write-gate.py — the Bash door onto the write policies that already exist.

WHY THIS EXISTS, proven in one session on 2026-08-09 rather than argued: the
linkedin-engagement-daily run wrote a vault markdown file with a `python3 -c`
command from Bash and it SUCCEEDED. Minutes later the identical change through
Edit was BLOCKED with record-home-gate.py's full refusal text. Nothing about the
content differed. THE SAME CONTENT WAS REFUSED OR ALLOWED PURELY BY WHICH TOOL
CARRIED IT, because every write gate here matches Write|Edit|MultiEdit and Bash
is a door none of them watch. Rule 14181e60 (database first) is enforced by
record-home-gate.py, so it held only against sessions that were not going to
break it anyway.

THE THREAT MODEL IS CARELESSNESS, NOT EVASION, and that is not a guess. The run
that found this had no intent to bypass anything: it reached for Bash because the
content carried URLs another guard had just refused, discovered the write gate
only when Edit refused a follow-up correction, and then stopped rather than
repeating it. An unintentional bypass by a compliant session is stronger evidence
that a control is mis-scoped than a deliberate one would be. A gate written
against a determined adversary would need to be complete or worthless; a gate
written against a convenient tool needs to cover the shapes people reach for.

THIS GATE DECIDES NOTHING, WHICH IS THE WHOLE DESIGN. Two gates already hold the
judgment about where a write may land — record-home-gate.py owns the vault,
one-repo-gate.py owns code outside the repo. A third policy for Bash would be the
two-homes disease one layer down, and the copies would drift the first time
either changed. So this file EXTRACTS candidate write targets from a shell
command and hands each one to those policies unchanged. One judgment, three
doors: rule a8c55a47 (a manual path and an automated path that do the same job
must be the same code) applied to tool doors rather than to scripts.

WHAT IT EXTRACTS, and each shape is here because it is one somebody reaches for:
  · redirections — `> f`, `>> f`, `>| f`, `&> f`, `2> f`, with or without a space
  · heredocs written to a file — `cat > f <<EOF`, which is the redirect above
  · `tee f` and `tee -a f`
  · `sed -i` over a named file
  · `cp` / `mv` / `install` destinations
  · `dd of=f`, `truncate f`
  · inline interpreters — `python -c`, `python3 -c`, `node -e`, and heredocs fed
    to them — scanned for path literals ONLY when the code also carries a write
    indicator, so a read-only one-liner is not caught

TOKENISED, NOT REGEXED OVER RAW TEXT, and that difference is the gate's
survival. `git commit -m "throughput a > b now"` contains a `>` that is not a
redirect. A raw regex fires on it, on every commit whose message contains a
comparison, and the gate gets switched off within a day. shlex sees one quoted
token and correctly finds no redirection.

WHAT IT DELIBERATELY IGNORES: /dev/* targets, `2>&1` and its relatives, reads of
any kind, and every path both delegated policies allow.

THE RESIDUAL, NAMED RATHER THAN HIDDEN. Extraction cannot be complete against
arbitrary shell. A path assembled from variables at runtime, an interpreter this
file does not know, a script invoked by name that writes on its own, a base64
payload decoded and executed — none are seen here. This closes the shapes that
are actually used, not the space of things that are possible. Anyone reading this
should treat it as raising the cost of an accidental bypass, never as proof that
one cannot happen. The complete control for that is enforcement at the filesystem
or at the record layer, which is a larger build and a separate decision.

FAILS CLOSED ON DENY, OPEN ON ERROR — exit 2 plus stderr, matching
guard-unattended.py and record-home-gate.py. A gate that wedges a session costs
more than the marginal safety of failing closed on a single-operator machine, so
any internal error allows the call.
"""

import importlib.util
import json
import os
import re
import shlex
import sys

REPO = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), ".."))
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
try:                                    # telemetry only — never load-bearing
    import hook_meter
    LOG = hook_meter.guard_log_path(REPO)
except Exception:                       # a missing meter must not change a verdict
    LOG = os.path.join(REPO, "out", "hook-guard.log")

REDIRECT = re.compile(r"^\d*&?>{1,2}\|?$")          # '>', '>>', '2>', '&>', '>|'
REDIRECT_ATTACHED = re.compile(r"^\d*&?>{1,2}\|?(?=\S)")
INTERPRETER_FLAG = {("python", "-c"), ("python3", "-c"), ("node", "-e"),
                    ("ruby", "-e"), ("perl", "-e")}
# A PATH INSIDE A WRITE CALL, not a path anywhere near one. The distinction cost
# a second false positive on the day this shipped.
#
# The first version paired two loose tests: "does this code contain any path
# literal" and, separately, "does this code contain any write indicator". Applied
# to a `python3 <<PY ... PY` heredoc it flagged a path the script only READ,
# because some other line in the same script wrote something else. A verification
# command of my own tripped it, which is how it was found — and it would fire on
# any script that reads one file and writes another, which is most scripts.
#
# Direction of error decides this, the same way it decided the unexpanded-variable
# case above: a false DENY blocks real work every time it fires, a false ALLOW
# only fails to catch something. So the path must sit INSIDE the write call
# itself. That still covers the shape this gate was built for — the 2026-08-09
# incident was `open("<vault file>","a").write(...)`, matched by the first pattern
# here — and it stops guessing about paths that merely appear nearby.
EMBEDDED_WRITE = [
    # open("PATH", "w"|"a"|"x"|"wb"…)
    re.compile(r"""open\s*\(\s*['"]([^'"\n]+)['"]\s*,\s*['"][awx]"""),
    # Path("PATH").write_text(…) / .write_bytes(…) / .open("w")
    re.compile(r"""Path\s*\(\s*['"]([^'"\n]+)['"]\s*\)\s*\.\s*(?:write_text|write_bytes|open\s*\(\s*['"][awx])"""),
    # fs.writeFileSync("PATH", …) / appendFileSync / createWriteStream
    re.compile(r"""(?:writeFileSync|appendFileSync|createWriteStream)\s*\(\s*['"]([^'"\n]+)['"]"""),
]


def log(line):
    try:
        os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(LOG), exist_ok=True)
        with open(LOG, "a") as fh:
            fh.write(f"bash-write-gate {line}\n")
    except Exception:
        pass


def load(module_name, filename):
    """Import a sibling gate so its POLICY is reused rather than reimplemented.

    Returns None on any failure, and the caller treats that as 'this policy has
    no opinion' — a missing sibling must not wedge Bash for the whole machine.
    """
    try:
        spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(
            module_name, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), filename))

command from Bash and it SUCCEEDED. Minutes later the identical change through
Edit was BLOCKED with record-home-gate.py's full refusal text. Nothing about the
content differed. THE SAME CONTENT WAS REFUSED OR ALLOWED PURELY BY WHICH TOOL

is a door none of them watch. Rule 14181e60 (database first) is enforced by
record-home-gate.py, so it held only against sessions that were not going to
break it anyway.

that found this had no intent to bypass anything: it reached for Bash because the
content carried URLs another guard had just refused, discovered the write gate
only when Edit refused a follow-up correction, and then stopped rather than
repeating it. An unintentional bypass by a compliant session is stronger evidence
that a control is mis-scoped than a deliberate one would be. A gate written
against a determined adversary would need to be complete or worthless; a gate
written against a convenient tool needs to cover the shapes people reach for.

THIS GATE DECIDES NOTHING, WHICH IS THE WHOLE DESIGN. Two gates already hold the
judgment about where a write may land — record-home-gate.py owns the vault,
one-repo-gate.py owns code outside the repo. A third policy for Bash would be the
two-homes disease one layer down, and the copies would drift the first time
either changed. So this file EXTRACTS candidate write targets from a shell
command and hands each one to those policies unchanged. One judgment, three
doors: rule a8c55a47 (a manual path and an automated path that do the same job
must be the same code) applied to tool doors rather than to scripts.

WHAT IT EXTRACTS, and each shape is here because it is one somebody reaches for:
  · redirections — `> f`, `>> f`, `>| f`, `&> f`, `2> f`, with or without a space
  · heredocs written to a file — `cat > f <<EOF`, which is the redirect above
  · `tee f` and `tee -a f`
  · `sed -i` over a named file
  · `cp` / `mv` / `install` destinations
  · `dd of=f`, `truncate f`

    indicator, so a read-only one-liner is not caught

survival. `git commit -m "throughput a > b now"` contains a `>` that is not a
redirect. A raw regex fires on it, on every commit whose message contains a
comparison, and the gate gets switched off within a day. shlex sees one quoted
token and correctly finds no redirection.

any kind, and every path both delegated policies allow.

arbitrary shell. A path assembled from variables at runtime, an interpreter this
file does not know, a script invoked by name that writes on its own, a base64
payload decoded and executed — none are seen here. This closes the shapes that
are actually used, not the space of things that are possible. Anyone reading this
should treat it as raising the cost of an accidental bypass, never as proof that
one cannot happen. The complete control for that is enforcement at the filesystem
or at the record layer, which is a larger build and a separate decision.

guard-unattended.py and record-home-gate.py. A gate that wedges a session costs
more than the marginal safety of failing closed on a single-operator machine, so

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""blocker-decider-gate.py — a capability blocker names its decider, or it
does not file (rule 88e9b5eb).

'NOT AUTHORIZED' AND 'NOT POSSIBLE' ARE DIFFERENT FINDINGS, and a loop row
that says blocker='capability' without saying which one it is hides exactly
the fact its reader needs. If someone COULD grant the credential, gate, or
verb, the row must name that person — in this system that is synthetic_operator or synthetic_operator —
because a grant nobody is asked for never arrives, and the loop rots as
"blocked" while the decider it is waiting on does not know it exists. If
NOBODY can grant it (the plan lacks the API, the surface has no such control),
the row must say so plainly, so it reads as a limit to design around rather
than a request to wait on.

So on add-loop with blocker='capability', the row's own text must carry one
of the two resolutions:

    a named decider    — synthetic_operator or synthetic_operator appears in the row's text
    a stated limit     — the text says it is impossible/cannot be granted,
                         rather than merely unauthorized

Everything else — other blocker classes, other verbs, malformed payloads —
passes untouched, and any internal error FAILS OPEN: a wedged filing is worse
than a vague one, and the deferral gate server-side still enforces the rest
of the row's shape.

PreToolUse deny (exit 2), same contract as escalation-gate.py beside it.
Fixtures: ops/blocker-decider-gate-selftest.py.
"""
import json
import os
import re
import sys

# synthetic_operator and synthetic_operator are the only grant-holders in this system. A word-boundary
# match anywhere in the row's text counts — "synthetic_operator grants it", "only synthetic_operator can",
# "synthetic_operator→synthetic_operator" all name the person whose queue this actually sits in.
DECIDER = re.compile(r"\b(synthetic_operator|synthetic_operator)\b", re.I)

# The other honest answer: nobody can grant it. Stated impossibility turns
# the row from a request into a recorded limit, which is allowed.
IMPOSSIBLE = re.compile(
    r"\b(impossible|cannot be granted|can'?t be granted|does not exist"
    r"|no such (api|control|permission|capability|feature)"
    r"|not (available|supported) on (this|the) plan|nobody can grant)\b", re.I)

TEXT_FIELDS = ("title", "body", "unblocks", "source_note", "blocker_detail")


def row_text(tool_input) -> str:
    if not isinstance(tool_input, dict):
        return ""
    return "\n".join(str(tool_input.get(f) or "") for f in TEXT_FIELDS
                     if tool_input.get(f))


def needs_decider(tool_input) -> bool:
    if not isinstance(tool_input, dict):
        return False
    if tool_input.get("blocker") != "capability":
        return False
    text = row_text(tool_input)
    return not (DECIDER.search(text) or IMPOSSIBLE.search(text))


REASON = (
    "BLOCKER-DECIDER GATE — refused. blocker='capability' without a decider "
    "is 'not authorized' and 'not possible' filed as the same finding "
    "(rule 88e9b5eb), and they are different findings.\n\n"
    "If someone can grant this capability, NAME THE DECIDER in the row — in "
    "this system that is synthetic_operator or synthetic_operator — so the request sits in a person's "
    "queue instead of rotting as 'blocked':\n\n"
    "    blocker_detail: \"needs the NEON_API_KEY only synthetic_operator holds — synthetic_operator "
    "grants it\"\n\n"
    "If nobody can grant it, SAY THAT PLAINLY (e.g. 'no such API on this "
    "plan — genuinely impossible'), so the row reads as a limit to design "
    "around, not a request nobody was asked for.\n"
)


def class_advisory(payload):
    """Show a recorder the defect classes that already exist, before it files.

    A SECOND CONCERN IN THIS FILE, hosted the way ops/command_precheck.py is
    hosted in delegation-gate.py and for the same reason: a new file under
    hooks/ carries a shebang, which makes it a sealed script entrypoint and
    costs a mutation-registry successor — a generated registry, a production
    migration, a fixture rebuilt from origin/main and a disposable PostgreSQL
    round trip. This gate is already registered on exactly the record verbs,
    already reads the same payload, and already runs under the repository
    interpreter, so hosting the dispatch here costs a re-digest of one row.

    WHY IT HAS TO BE A HOOK AT ALL, which is the whole point. The record-defect
    verb's own schema text already asks a session to reuse an existing class.
    The ledger holds 304 singletons across 320 classes. Asking works sometimes;
    a door that opens on the way past works every time.

    IT CANNOT AFFECT THIS GATE. It runs before the blocker logic, catches
    everything, and returns on any failure — no credential, no service, no
    database, bad payload, missing library. The refusal path below is untouched
    either way, and a session that files a defect while the judgment is down
    files it exactly as it does today.
    """
    tool = payload.get("tool_name") or payload.get("toolName") or ""
    if not (tool.startswith("mcp__") and tool.endswith("__record-defect")):
        return
    ti = payload.get("tool_input") or payload.get("toolInput") or {}
    if not isinstance(ti, dict):
        return
    # claimed and actual are the verb's own two required fields — a defect row
    # that states no contradiction is a note, not a defect — and they are what
    # the ranking reads. It scores a class by the contradiction it describes,
    # so passing the class name alone would throw away the half that separates
    # a near-duplicate from a genuine reuse.
    claimed, actual = ti.get("claimed"), ti.get("actual")
    # Both must be real, non-empty strings. Not str(): str(None) is "None" and
    # str(["a"]) is "['a']", each of them truthy, so coercing would send junk
    # to a paid service and rank a defect class against the word None.
    if not (isinstance(claimed, str) and claimed.strip()
            and isinstance(actual, str) and actual.strip()):
        return
    proposed = {"claimed": claimed, "actual": actual}
    try:
        import importlib.util
        spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(
            "jev_defect_class",
            os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))),
                         "ops", "jev_defect_class.py"))
        if spec is None or spec.loader is None:
            return
        module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
        spec.loader.exec_module(module)
        note = module.advise(proposed)
        if note:
            print(json.dumps({"hookSpecificOutput": {
                "hookEventName": "PreToolUse", "additionalContext": note}}))
    except Exception:
        return


def main():
    try:
        payload = json.load(sys.stdin)
    except Exception:
        sys.exit(0)

    class_advisory(payload)

    try:
        tool = payload.get("tool_name") or payload.get("toolName") or ""
        if not (tool.startswith("mcp__") and tool.endswith("__add-loop")):
            sys.exit(0)
        ti = payload.get("tool_input") or payload.get("toolInput") or {}
        if not needs_decider(ti):
            sys.exit(0)
        print(REASON, file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(2)
    except SystemExit:
        raise
    except Exception:
        sys.exit(0)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
chat-lint-carryover.py — deliver the chat lint's findings BEFORE the next reply
is written, instead of blocking the last one after synthetic_operator has already read it.

WHY THIS EXISTS. synthetic_operator, 2026-08-16: "why does every claude session now repeat its
responses twice? bc all its doing is chewing up my tokens." He was right, and
his follow-up named the fix: "what if we change the gate so that it doesn't
trigger a restate in the first place."

THE MECHANISM, and its hard ceiling. There is no PreAssistantMessage deny in
Claude Code — hooks/conduct-stop-gate.py documents this and it was live-probed
on this machine 2026-08-09. A reply cannot be caught before synthetic_operator sees it. The
only lever is a Stop hook returning {"decision":"block"}, and a block by
definition forces ANOTHER assistant message. So for a WORDING violation the
trade is bad: the banned word already reached him, it cannot be unsent, and
blocking buys nothing except a second copy of a message he owns.

THE SPLIT THIS ENFORCES, which is the real rule:
  - A gate catching UNDONE WORK (a command handed over instead of run, a
    verification never performed) SHOULD block. The next message is the result
    of work, not a restatement, and blocking is the only thing that gets the
    work done. That is hooks/conduct-stop-gate.py and it still blocks.
  - A gate catching WORDING only should NOT block. It records the finding and
    this hook injects it as context on the next UserPromptSubmit, so the very
    next reply is written correctly. Cost: a few lines of context, once, and
    only when there was a violation. No extra message, ever.

FAIL-OPEN, always. A missing note, an unreadable file, a bad path — all exit 0
silently. A writing-style reminder is never worth breaking a turn over.
"""
import json
import os
import re
import sys

REPO = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))


def repo_root():
    """The repo root, from CARR_REPO_ROOT env or script-relative.

    Same contract as hooks/chat-lint-gate.py's repo_root(): the selftest sets
    CARR_REPO_ROOT so concurrent runs never share one out/chat-lint-carry
    directory. Production leaves the variable unset.
    """
    env = os.environ.get("CARR_REPO_ROOT")
    if env and os.path.isdir(env):
        return os.path.realpath(env)
    return REPO


def carry_path(session):
    safe = re.sub(r"[^A-Za-z0-9_.-]", "_", str(session or "unknown"))[:64]
    return os.path.join(repo_root(), "out", "chat-lint-carry", f"{safe}.txt")


def main():
    try:
        payload = json.load(sys.stdin)
    except Exception:
        return 0

    try:
        path = carry_path(payload.get("session_id"))
        if not os.path.exists(path):
            return 0
        with open(path) as fh:
            note = fh.read().strip()
        # Consume it either way: a note that survives its delivery would be
        # re-injected on every following turn.
        try:
            os.remove(path)
        except Exception:
            pass
        if not note:
            return 0
        print(json.dumps({
            "hookSpecificOutput": {
                "hookEventName": "UserPromptSubmit",
                "additionalContext": note,
            }
        }))
    except Exception:
        return 0
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
